pages.hook: On Shark Tank India, the question founders get asked most often is not about valuation — it is "monthly burn kitna hai?" Sharks ask it because a great story with a broken burn is still a dead business. Skippi Ice Pops halved its burn after the show and then grew 40x. Your burn rate and your runway are the two numbers that decide how much time you really have.
what: Burn rate is how much cash your business spends each month beyond what it earns. There are two versions: gross burn, the total spend, and net burn, the spend minus income. Net burn is the honest number, because it is what actually drains your bank account every month.

If you spend ₹5 lakh a month and earn ₹2 lakh, your net burn is ₹3 lakh. If you have ₹30 lakh in the bank, you have ten months of runway. Tank Metrics shows both the net burn and the runway in ₹ Lakhs, the way an Indian founder checks their own account, not in dollars.

Runway is the second half of the same question. Burn tells you how fast the money is leaving; runway tells you how many months that leaves you. A founder who knows both can raise the next round from a position of strength instead of from panic.

A useful habit is to write the burn and the runway down on the first of every month, before the invoices arrive. It takes two minutes and it turns a vague worry into a number you can act on. Founders who do this catch a rising burn two or three months early, which is exactly the window where a small fix is still cheap.

formula.expr: Net Burn = Monthly Expenses − Monthly Income
formula.note: Runway in months = Cash in Bank ÷ Net Burn.

example.intro: Three Indian startups, three very different months, all measured in ₹ Lakhs.
example.outro: The last row is the goal: when income passes expenses, burn disappears and the business funds itself. Skippi did exactly this — it cut its burn in half and became sustainable, and the growth followed. Track your net burn every single month, small or large.

Type this month's total income in ₹ lakh. Zero is fine if you are pre-revenue.
Step 2 - Enter monthly expenses
Add salaries, rent, marketing and taxes into one monthly figure in ₹ lakh.
Step 3 - Read burn and runway
The calculator shows net burn and how many months of cash you have left, in ₹ Lakhs.
why_india: An Indian startup carries monthly liabilities that US burn tools ignore: GST, TDS and PF payments. Left out of the expense figure, they make the burn look smaller than it is. Adding them back gives the true picture of an Indian founder's month.

In India, a runway of more than twelve months is considered safe, because closing a funding round here takes three to six months. A US benchmark of six months is too tight for India. Tank Metrics keeps the runway and the burn in rupees, with the Indian timeline in mind.

India also has strong seasonal cash swings. The festive months bring revenue and the months after bring returns and slower sales, so a single month's burn can flatter the picture. An average of three months gives a truer runway than any one month does.
faqs: How do you calculate burn rate?
Net Burn = Monthly Expenses − Monthly Income. If expenses are ₹5 lakh and income is ₹2 lakh, the net burn is ₹3 lakh a month.
How much runway should a startup have?
Indian startups should keep at least twelve months of runway, because a new round takes three to six months to close. Under six months is the danger zone.
What is the difference between gross burn and net burn?
Gross burn is the total spend; net burn is spend minus income. Net burn is the real number because it shows how fast your cash is falling.

pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 3, Decode Age took ₹1.5 crore for 2.25% equity plus a 1% royalty until ₹1 crore was recouped. A royalty deal gives the shark downside protection and lets the founder keep more equity, but it also takes a slice of every month's sales. This calculator shows you the real break-even between a royalty deal and a plain equity deal, in ₹ Crores.
what: A royalty deal means the investor takes a smaller equity stake plus a percentage of sales (a royalty) until a fixed amount is recouped. After that, the royalty stops and only the equity remains. It became common on Shark Tank India from Season 3 as a way to close a gap when founders and sharks disagree on valuation.

A pure equity deal takes equity only. A royalty deal saves equity up front but charges your cash flow every month. Tank Metrics puts the two side by side so you can see how many months the royalty runs and what it costs in total, all in ₹ Lakhs and ₹ Crores.

The trade is simple to state. A royalty deal buys you a smaller equity cut today and charges you a monthly slice of sales until the recoup is complete. Whether that is cheap or expensive depends entirely on how fast your sales grow from here.

One rule of thumb helps here. If the royalty would take more than about three years to recoup at your current sales, the deal is leaning toward the investor. If it recoups in under a year, the founder is giving away cash that pure equity might have cost less to part with. The right answer sits between those two ends.

formula.expr: Months to Recoup = Recoup Amount ÷ (Monthly Sales × Royalty %)
formula.note: Effective cost = equity given + total royalty paid until the recoup is complete.

faqs: What is a Shark Tank royalty deal?

In a royalty deal the investor takes less equity but also a percentage of sales (a royalty) until the invested amount is recouped. For example, ₹1.5 crore for 2.25% equity plus 1% royalty until ₹1 crore is recouped.
Is a royalty deal good or bad for a founder?

It depends. It can save equity if sales grow fast and the royalty ends soon. If sales are slow, the royalty runs long and the total cost can exceed a pure equity deal, so calculate the break-even first.
What happens after the royalty is recouped?
Once the recoup amount is fully paid, the royalty stops and the investor keeps only the equity. That is why the recoup time matters so much.

pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 3, a founder said he was valued at ₹4 crore. A shark offered ₹1 crore for 20% and corrected him on camera: the post-money valuation is ₹5 crore, not ₹4 crore. what: Pre-money and post-money are the two valuations of the same deal, separated by the investment. Post-money is what the company is worth after the cheque lands; pre-money is post-money minus the cheque. The investor's equity is always a slice of the post-money number, never the pre-money one.

pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 3, a D2C brand came with a confident pitch about growth and repeat buyers. Then a shark asked the one question that ends most pitches: what is your LTV to CAC? The founder did not have the number. Every rupee spent winning a customer has to come back several times over for growth to build a business instead of burning one. This calculator gives you that number for your D2C or SaaS business in seconds, in ₹.
what: The LTV:CAC ratio puts two numbers side by side: what a customer is worth to you over their whole life (LTV), and what it cost to win them (CAC). Divide one by the other and you get the single figure investors in Indian D2C and SaaS ask for first.

A ratio of 3:1 or better is the common rule of thumb. Below 1:1 you lose money on every customer you win; between 1 and 3 you are spending too much to grow. A D2C brand with an LTV of ₹4,500 and a CAC of ₹1,500 is at 3:1 - healthy. A quick-commerce brand with ₹800 of LTV and ₹1,200 of CAC is at 0.67:1 - it loses money on every order.

The ratio only means something when both sides are measured the same way. LTV should be built on gross-margin profit, not revenue, and CAC should include ads, salaries and agency fees - not just the ad bill. Measure one side generously and the other tightly and the ratio lies.

formula.expr: LTV : CAC = Lifetime Value ÷ Customer Acquisition Cost
formula.note: Use profit-based LTV and fully-loaded CAC. An LTV of ₹4,500 over a ₹1,500 CAC gives 3 : 1. Below 1:1 the business loses money on every customer; 3:1 and above is the range investors look for.

why_india: Indian D2C founders usually track revenue and order counts, not unit economics, because that is what the marketplace dashboard shows. The LTV:CAC ratio forces the two numbers that decide survival onto one screen.

Indian SaaS companies often bill in dollars but pay for talent and ads in rupees, so the ratio gets distorted if the two sides are converted carelessly. Keep both sides in ₹ over the same period and the number is honest.

Indian investors have become far stricter about this ratio since the funding winter - a 1.2:1 pitch that raised money in 2021 does not raise it now. Having the number ready, and honest, is the difference between a second meeting and a polite no.
mistakes: Using revenue-based LTV against a fully-loaded CAC, which makes a loss-making business look healthy.
Leaving sales salaries and agency fees out of CAC, so the cost of winning a customer looks far lower than it is.

faqs: What is a good LTV to CAC ratio in India?

Every cost of winning a customer: ad spend, the sales team's salaries, agency fees and introductory discounts - divided by the new customers won in the same period.

pages.hook: In Shark Tank India Season 1, a founder gave away 20% for ₹1 crore and felt lucky. Two years later a second round took another 20%, and an ESOP pool for senior hires took 10% more. The founder who once owned the whole company was now under 60% - and had never once sat down and multiplied it out. Dilution compounds, and each round is charged against a smaller and smaller base. This calculator shows what you keep after the round, the ESOP pool, and the rupees of company you actually gave up.
what: Dilution is the slice of the company a founder gives away, and the slice that is left. If you own 100% today and hand an investor 10%, you keep 90%. That part is simple - the part that catches founders out is what happens across several rounds and an ESOP pool.

Dilution compounds because each round is charged against a smaller base. Lose 10% in round one and you are at 90%. Lose 20% in round two and you are at 72%, not 70%. Add a 10% ESOP pool and you are at 64.8%. A founder who started with everything can end up below two-thirds without a single round looking large.

The number that matters is not the stake alone but the stake next to the valuation. Giving 20% at a high price can cost less of the company's value than giving 5% at a low one. This calculator shows the stake after the round, the ESOP pool, and the total equity given up, so the trade-off is visible before the term sheet is signed.

formula.expr: Founder Equity After = Equity Before × (1 − Equity Given ÷ 100) × (1 − ESOP Pool ÷ 100)
formula.note: Multiply, do not subtract, across rounds. 100% after a 10% round is 90%; a further 20% round leaves 72%, not 70%. The ESOP pool dilutes founders exactly like an investor does.

why_india: Indian founder agreements often create the ESOP pool before the round rather than after, which means the pool dilutes the founders and not the incoming investor. That ordering is a real difference from many US deals and it changes the final number.

Indian rounds frequently use CCPS (Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares) with anti-dilution clauses, and a down round can trigger them - meaning the founder's dilution is larger than the headline percentage suggests.

Indian family businesses that bring in an outside investor rarely write down how the founding family's stake will move across future rounds. This calculator is how you show your CA and your family exactly where the stake lands.
mistakes: Subtracting percentages across rounds instead of multiplying fractions, which understates the total dilution.
Forgetting the ESOP pool, which dilutes founders exactly like an investor does and is often created before the round.
Watching the stake and ignoring the valuation - giving 20% at a high price can cost less than 5% at a low one.
faqs: How do I calculate founder dilution?
Multiply, do not subtract. Equity after a round = equity before × (1 − equity given). 100% after a 10% round is 90%; a further 20% round leaves 72%.
Does the ESOP pool dilute founders?
Yes. The employee option pool is carved out of the cap table and dilutes founders exactly like an investor's stake does, unless the deal says otherwise.
How much dilution is normal per round in India?
Seed rounds typically take 10-20%, Series A another 15-25%. Across three rounds a founder can end up holding 50-65% of the company, which is normal and not a failure.

Subtract monthly revenue from monthly expenses. With ₹12 lakh of expenses and ₹7 lakh of revenue, the net burn is ₹5 lakh a month.

To get it, start with revenue and subtract the operating expenses, which means salaries, rent, marketing, raw material and everything else needed to run the business day to day. pages.hook: Founders on Shark Tank India are asked one personal question almost every time, what salary do you draw? The honest answers are all over the place. Some founders take nothing, others pay themselves a modest ₹50,000 a month, and a few admit to a comfortable figure once the business is profitable. Bamboo India took a deal at ₹50 lakh for 3.5% equity plus ₹30 lakh of debt, and the sharks pressed on whether the founders were drawing a salary from a business of that size. This calculator shows the take-home you need and whether your profit can actually afford it.
what: A founder salary calculator startup India use turns two numbers into a decision. The first is the monthly take-home you actually need to live on, and the second is the annual profit the company can genuinely spare. Multiply your take-home by twelve to get the salary the company must pay, then compare it with profit. If the salary is a small slice of profit, the business can afford it, but if it eats most of the profit, you are funding your lifestyle from the company's runway.

The calculator also shows the largest salary that still looks healthy, taken as half of annual profit, so the business keeps enough to reinvest. In a young Indian startup this balance matters more than the headline number, because every rupee paid as salary is a rupee not spent on growth or left as a buffer.

Founder salary is also a tax question, not just a cash question. A salary paid to a founder-director is a business expense that reduces the company's taxable profit, and it is taxed in the founder's own hands as salary income, usually with TDS deducted at source. How you split pay between salary and dividends changes the total tax bill.

There is no single correct salary. The right figure is the smallest amount that lets you focus fully on the business without worrying about rent or school fees. A founder who is distracted by money cannot build well, and a founder who overpays weakens the very company that pays them. This tool helps you find that middle ground with two numbers you already know.

why_india: In India the choice between salary and dividends is a real tax decision. Salary is deductible for the company and taxed in the founder's hands at slab rates, while dividends are paid from post-tax profit and then taxed again in the shareholder's hands. A chartered accountant can model both, and the right answer depends on your slab.

Indian founders also carry obligations a US template ignores. A founder-director drawing a salary may need to contribute to PF and other statutory dues, and the salary must be reasonable for the work, or the tax officer can question it at assessment.

Many Indian startups begin with the founder taking almost no salary and living on savings. That is fine for a while, but a business that cannot pay its founder a fair wage is fragile, and investors on the show treat a sane salary as a sign of discipline rather than weakness.
faqs: How much salary should a founder take in India?
Enough to live on, but small enough to leave the business room to grow. A common guide is to keep it under half of annual profit so the company can still reinvest.
Is founder salary tax deductible?
Yes. A salary paid to a founder-director is a business expense that reduces the company's taxable profit, and it is taxed in the founder's own hands as salary income.
Should a founder take salary or dividends?

Salary is deductible for the company and taxed at your slab, while dividends are paid from post-tax profit and taxed again in your hands. A chartered accountant can compare the two for your situation.
